title: THE SEXUAL SCANDAL THE CHURCH REFUSED TO CONFRONT—AND THE TERRIFYING REASON PAUL SAID SILENCE WAS NOT LOVE
paragraphs: THE SEXUAL SCANDAL THE CHURCH REFUSED TO CONFRONT—AND THE TERRIFYING REASON PAUL SAID SILENCE WAS NOT LOVE

One man was living in open sexual sin. An entire congregation was looking the other way. Then the apostle Paul wrote words that shattered their comfortable silence. But behind his shocking command was something far more powerful than punishment: the desperate hope that a sinner might still be saved.
There was a man sitting among the believers in Corinth who probably knew the songs, recognized the prayers, and understood exactly when to say “Amen.”
He may have greeted people at the door. He may have listened to Scripture being read. He may even have spoken confidently about the grace of God.
But there was something terribly wrong.
He was involved in a sexual relationship with his father's wife.
And the most disturbing part of the story?
The church knew.
They knew enough for the apostle Paul to hear about it from a distance.
Yet instead of grieving, instead of confronting the situation, instead of calling the man to repentance, the congregation had somehow continued with an attitude of spiritual pride.
Imagine walking into that gathering.
People are talking about faith. Someone is speaking about freedom in Christ. Others are celebrating their spiritual maturity.
And somewhere among them is a scandal everyone knows about but apparently nobody wants to address.
Perhaps some were afraid of confrontation.
Perhaps others had confused grace with permission.
Perhaps they were so proud of their tolerance that they no longer recognized the difference between welcoming a sinner and approving of ongoing sin.
We cannot know every motive in that congregation.
But we know what Paul saw.
And what he saw horrified him.
Because sometimes the greatest danger to a church is not the sin everyone can see.
It is the spiritual blindness that convinces everyone they no longer need to confront it.
Listen to how Paul begins:
"It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife." — 1 Corinthians 5:1, KJV
The Greek is even more revealing.
Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia.
The opening means, in context, that sexual immorality is actually being reported among them.

The word πορνεία (porneia) refers broadly to illicit sexual activity. Here Paul identifies the specific offense: a man has his father's wife, an expression naturally understood as referring to his stepmother.
The wording does not establish whether his father was still alive, nor does it explain every circumstance of the relationship. But the moral issue was unmistakable.
Leviticus 18:8 had already forbidden sexual relations with one's father's wife. Leviticus 20:11 likewise treated the offense with extraordinary seriousness under Israel's law.
Paul was not inventing a new sexual standard because he disliked someone.
He was confronting behavior that Scripture had already identified as profoundly wrong.
And then he said something that should make every modern congregation uncomfortable.
"And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned..." — 1 Corinthians 5:2, KJV
Puffed up.
Proud.
Self-satisfied.
The Greek word behind that expression comes from φυσιόω (physioō), meaning to puff up or become arrogant.
Paul had already challenged the Corinthians' pride elsewhere in the letter.
Now their arrogance had become particularly dangerous.
Because they were apparently congratulating themselves while a fellow believer remained trapped in destructive sin.
And Paul asked, in effect:
Why are you proud when you should be grieving?
Why are you celebrating when someone among you is spiritually endangered?
Why are you treating this like a minor inconvenience when the Gospel calls you to something much deeper?
That question reaches far beyond ancient Corinth.
It reaches into churches where leaders protect reputations instead of people.
It reaches into Christian communities where obvious wrongdoing is quietly tolerated because the person involved is influential, generous, popular, or connected.
It reaches into families where everyone knows something is wrong, but nobody wants to be the first to speak.
And perhaps most painfully, it reaches into our own hearts.
Because we know what it feels like to want grace without correction.
We know what it feels like to hope nobody notices the compromise we have learned to live with.
We know what it feels like to say, "God understands," when what we really mean is, "I do not want to surrender this."
But here is where the story becomes uncomfortable in a different way.
Paul did not tell the church to hate the man.
He did not command them to spread gossip, humiliate him publicly, or enjoy watching his life collapse.
He told them they should have mourned.
The Greek verb is related to πενθέω (pentheō), a word associated with grief and lamentation.
Think about that.
Before Paul speaks of removing the man from their fellowship, he confronts the absence of sorrow.
Not excitement over exposing someone.
Not satisfaction at catching someone.
Not the thrill of having a scandal to discuss.
Grief.
Because when someone is destroying himself spiritually, love should not respond with entertainment.
It should respond with tears.
There is an enormous difference between a church that confronts sin because it loves righteousness and a church that exposes people because it loves scandal.
One seeks restoration.
The other enjoys humiliation.
And only one reflects the heart of Christ.
But Paul did not stop at telling them to grieve.
He gave a command that sounds almost unbearable to modern ears.
"To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus." — 1 Corinthians 5:5, KJV
Read that final phrase again.
That the spirit may be saved.
Not so that the congregation could feel superior.
Not so that everyone could celebrate the man's downfall.
Not so that his name would become a permanent warning attached to his worst decision.
That his spirit might be saved.
The Greek reads:
ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου
Hina to pneuma sōthē en tē hēmera tou kyriou.
"That the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord."
There it is.
The purpose beneath the severity.
The hope beneath the heartbreak.
The redemptive aim behind a command that sounds, at first, like rejection.
Paul wanted the man to be rescued.
But rescue would require confronting a reality the congregation had refused to face.
What does delivering someone to Satan mean?
Within the context of 1 Corinthians 5, the clearest practical expression is removal from the fellowship of the church.
Paul's later command is explicit:
"Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person." — 1 Corinthians 5:13, KJV
The language reflects the distinction between the gathered community of believers and the world outside it.
The church was to stop treating a persistently unrepentant person as though his conduct were consistent with faithful Christian fellowship.

Interpreters differ over the precise meaning of "destruction of the flesh." Some understand it as severe bodily suffering; others emphasize the breaking of sinful, fleshly patterns through discipline. The passage does not authorize us to declare that the church possesses power to inflict physical harm.
And whatever the precise mechanism, Paul's stated purpose remains clear.
Salvation, not revenge.
Repentance, not cruelty.
The recovery of a soul, not the destruction of a person for public satisfaction.
The church was not being told to become an executioner.
It was being told to stop pretending that everything was spiritually healthy.
And there is a truth here that many of us would rather avoid.
Sometimes love must become uncomfortable before repentance becomes possible.
Imagine a father watching his son walk toward the edge of a cliff.
The son is smiling.
He is confident.
He insists that he knows what he is doing.
Would the father prove his love by remaining silent?
Would he whisper, "I support whatever makes you happy," while watching his child approach destruction?
Or would he cry out?
Would he risk being misunderstood?
Would he risk hearing, "You are judging me"?
Would he run toward the danger because the life of his son matters more than the comfort of the moment?
That is not a perfect analogy for every church-discipline situation. Church leaders are fallible, and confrontation can be abused.
But it reveals something essential.
Biblical love is not simply the willingness to make someone feel accepted.
It is also the willingness to tell the truth when silence would leave them in danger.
And yet this is exactly where another warning must be heard.
Not everyone who claims to be defending holiness is acting like Jesus.
Some people use Scripture as a weapon because they enjoy controlling others.
Some expose private failures without biblical justification.
Some confuse personal suspicion with established wrongdoing.
Some protect powerful offenders while disciplining vulnerable people.
That is not the righteousness Paul was calling for.
The same apostle who demanded accountability also wrote:
"Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted." — Galatians 6:1, KJV
Restore.
In meekness.
While remembering your own vulnerability.
The Greek verb καταρτίζετε (katartizete) carries the sense of putting something right, restoring, or bringing it into proper condition.
The goal is not to crush the fallen.
It is to seek their restoration.
And Jesus Himself taught a process of correction in Matthew 18:15–17 that ordinarily begins privately and proceeds carefully.

First Corinthians 5 addresses a reported, openly scandalous situation involving a professing member of the church and a congregation that had failed to respond appropriately. It is not a license to publicize every private sin or bypass careful examination of facts.

Church discipline must never be confused with harassment, coercion, or the concealment of abuse. Where someone has been harmed, protecting victims and involving appropriate civil authorities when required are essential responsibilities, not betrayals of Christian unity.
True holiness does not protect an institution at the expense of the wounded.
True holiness submits everyone, including leaders, to the truth.
And if a church cannot distinguish between restoring a repentant sinner and protecting an unrepentant offender, something is terribly wrong.
But Paul goes even deeper.
He uses an image that would have been immediately recognizable to people familiar with the biblical Passover.
"Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?" — 1 Corinthians 5:6, KJV
A little leaven.
The whole lump.
In ordinary baking, leaven works its way through dough.
Paul uses that familiar process as a warning about the spreading influence of tolerated wrongdoing.
The danger was not simply one person's conduct.
It was what the congregation's approval, indifference, or arrogance could communicate to everyone else.
If openly unrepentant sin could be treated as spiritually harmless, what would the church eventually believe about repentance?
What would younger believers learn?
What would wounded people conclude about righteousness?
What would happen to a community that proclaimed transformation through Christ while refusing to acknowledge behavior that contradicted its confession?
Paul's answer was urgent.
"Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump..." — 1 Corinthians 5:7, KJV
But then comes the phrase that changes the entire emotional direction of the passage.
"For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us."
There.
In the middle of a chapter about sexual scandal, church discipline, and serious judgment, Paul brings the congregation back to Jesus Christ.
Not merely to rules.
Not merely to reputation.
Not merely to moral standards.
To the Lamb.
To the sacrifice.
To the blood.
To the cross.
Why?
Because Christian holiness does not begin with human superiority.
It begins with divine mercy.
The church is not a gathering of people who have never sinned.
It is a people called out of darkness by the Savior who died for sinners.
And that changes everything.
We do not confront sin because we believe we are too good to fall.
We confront it because we know what sin costs.
We know that our own salvation required the death of the sinless Son of God.
We know that forgiveness is not cheap.
And we know that the grace that pardons us also calls us into a new life.
The same Christ who welcomed the broken also commanded repentance.
The same Jesus who refused to condemn the woman brought before Him in John 8:1–11 also told her to leave her life of sin.
His mercy was not permission to remain unchanged.
His mercy opened the door to transformation.
And this is where the story stops being merely about Corinth.
Because there may be someone reading this who has spent years hiding behind the language of grace.
You know the verses about forgiveness.
You know the songs about mercy.
You know how to reassure yourself that God loves you.
And He does.
But deep down, you also know there is something you have been refusing to surrender.
Perhaps it is sexual compromise.
Perhaps it is an affair you keep promising to end.
Perhaps it is pornography you have hidden behind passwords and deleted histories.
Perhaps it is dishonesty, manipulation, bitterness, or a double life nobody at church suspects.
You have learned to live in two worlds.
One where you speak about Jesus.
And another where you protect the very thing He is calling you to leave behind.
And the exhausting part is not simply the secret.
It is the distance you feel between the person you present and the person you know you have become.
You can smile in a photograph and feel ashamed in the silence afterward.
You can worship on Sunday and spend Monday bargaining with temptation.
You can tell people, "God is good," while quietly wondering whether you have gone too far to come back.
But listen carefully.
The fact that your sin needs confronting does not mean your story is beyond redemption.
The cross tells us the opposite.
Jesus did not die because human beings needed a little improvement.
He died because sinners needed a Savior.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were sinners.
Not after we cleaned everything up.
Not after we became respectable.
Not after our reputation was repaired.
While we were sinners.
And yet the grace that meets us in our sin does not invite us to build a permanent home there.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
And sometimes grace confronts the very thing we are terrified to release.
Now consider another question.
Did Paul tell the Corinthians to separate themselves from every immoral person in society?
No.
In fact, he specifically corrected that misunderstanding.
"I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators: Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world..." — 1 Corinthians 5:9–10, KJV
Paul explains that avoiding every sinner outside the church would require leaving the world altogether.
His instruction concerned someone who claimed to be a brother while persisting in serious, unrepentant wrongdoing.
That distinction matters enormously.
Paul was not commanding Christians to despise unbelievers.
He was not telling the church to isolate itself from people who needed the Gospel.
He was insisting that those who profess allegiance to Christ must not treat their profession as a shield against accountability.
"For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within?" — 1 Corinthians 5:12, KJV
The church has responsibilities toward its own community that differ from its responsibilities toward those outside it.
And those responsibilities must be exercised with humility, fairness, truth, and a genuine desire for restoration.
We cannot demand that the world live as though it has already surrendered to Christ.
But neither can the church preach repentance while pretending repentance is optional for its own members.
This is not about making Christians appear morally superior.
It is about refusing to turn the name of Jesus into a religious disguise for deliberate hypocrisy.
And then comes a question that has haunted readers of this passage for centuries.
What happened to the man?
Did he repent?
Did he return?
Did the congregation eventually welcome him back?
First Corinthians 5 does not tell us.
But there is another passage worth considering.
In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul speaks of someone who had received punishment from the majority and urges the church to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love toward that person.
"Contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow." — 2 Corinthians 2:7, KJV
Some interpreters have understood this person to be the same man addressed in 1 Corinthians 5.
Others believe Paul was discussing a different offender connected to a separate conflict.
Scripture does not explicitly identify the two individuals as the same person, so we should not present that connection as established fact.
But the principle in 2 Corinthians is unmistakable.
When discipline has accomplished its proper purpose and repentance is evident, the church must not become addicted to punishment.
Forgive.
Comfort.
Reaffirm love.
Do not allow a person to be swallowed by excessive sorrow.
Can you see the heart of the Gospel in that?
The church must not call evil good.
But it must also never act as though a repentant sinner is beyond the reach of mercy.
There is a time to confront.
There is a time to mourn.
There is a time to establish boundaries.
And there is a time to open the door to restored fellowship when genuine repentance makes restoration appropriate and safe.
A congregation that refuses to confront destructive sin has misunderstood grace.
But a congregation that refuses to forgive the repentant has misunderstood grace just as badly.
Both errors forget Jesus.
And perhaps that is why this chapter remains so painfully relevant.
We live in a world where scandals can become entertainment within minutes.
A person's failure becomes a screenshot.
A private humiliation becomes a public spectacle.
People who have never met the individual suddenly speak with absolute confidence about motives, guilt, and what punishment is deserved.
Some call it accountability.
Others call it justice.
But not everything that goes viral is righteous.
And not every public accusation is true.
The Gospel calls us to something more demanding than outrage.
It calls us to truth without cruelty.
Accountability without arrogance.
Compassion without compromise.
Mercy without denial.
And restoration without pretending that consequences never existed.
Because Jesus Christ is neither indifferent to sin nor unwilling to save sinners.
Look at Peter.
He denied knowing Jesus three times.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And after the rooster crowed, Peter wept bitterly.
Imagine the shame.
He had promised loyalty.
He had spoken boldly.
He had believed himself stronger than he really was.
And when the moment of testing came, he collapsed.
Yet the risen Jesus did not abandon Peter to the worst night of his life.
In John 21, Jesus met him again, questioned him about his love, and entrusted him with responsibility to care for His sheep.
Peter's failure was real.
His grief was real.
But so was Christ's restoring mercy.
That is not the same situation as the scandal in Corinth, and we should not pretend the details are identical.
But both passages reveal something precious about the character of our Savior.
Jesus does not need to deny our failures in order to redeem our lives.
He tells the truth about sin.
And He has the power to bring sinners home.
Maybe that is the word someone needs today.
Not another excuse.
Not another comforting lie.
Not another voice telling you that the thing destroying your peace is harmless.
Perhaps what you need is the courage to say:
"Lord, I have been hiding."
"I have called my compromise freedom."
"I have confused Your patience with Your approval."
"I have defended what I should have confessed."
"And I am tired of running."
If those words describe you, remember the promise of 1 John 1:9:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
That promise is not a reward for pretending.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
Confession does not mean broadcasting intimate details to strangers or exposing yourself to unsafe people.
It means bringing your sin honestly before God and, where appropriate, seeking accountable, trustworthy pastoral care and taking concrete steps to repair harm.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what happened.
It is turning toward God, away from sin, and toward the life Christ calls us to live.
And if you have hurt someone, genuine repentance also means refusing to use forgiveness as a way to escape responsibility.
Grace does not erase every earthly consequence.
But it does mean that shame does not have to be the final author of your story.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because sin is imaginary.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because the crucified and risen Jesus is greater than the darkness from which He saves us.
And if this message has reached a place in your heart you have kept hidden, do not rush past it.
Stay there for a moment.
Ask yourself what you have been defending that God has been calling you to surrender.
Ask whether you have been silent when someone needed loving correction.
Ask whether you have been harsh when someone needed patient restoration.
Ask whether you have become more concerned with protecting the image of Christianity than demonstrating the character of Christ.
And above all, ask whether you have truly entrusted your life to Jesus, rather than merely becoming familiar with Christian language.
Because knowing how to speak about grace is not the same as surrendering to the Savior who gives it.
I would love for this conversation to become more than another article people read and forget.
And if the Lord is teaching you that correction and mercy belong together, share what He is showing you. Your testimony might help another believer realize that repentance is not the end of hope.
You do not need to reveal private details to be honest about your need for Jesus.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who may need this message.
Maybe a brother who has quietly drifted away.
Maybe a sister who thinks her past has permanently disqualified her from God's love.
Maybe a parent who is struggling to confront a loved one without losing compassion.
Maybe someone who has stopped attending church because the people who were supposed to reflect Jesus wounded them instead.
Because there may come a day when you need to remember that correction does not have to mean rejection, and that Christ's mercy is never an excuse to remain enslaved to sin.
Before we close, there is something personal I want to share with those who believe this ministry should continue reaching more people.
Gospel Warrior is not simply about publishing words on a screen.
The desire behind this work is to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, confront what needs to change, and discover the hope of Jesus Christ.
We want these resources and messages to keep reaching people who are spiritually hungry, discouraged, searching, or quietly struggling.
Scripture teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Not grudgingly.
Not under pressure.
Not because someone has made you feel guilty.
But willingly, thoughtfully, and with love for the Lord.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as everyday reminders of the truth we are called to live and share.
Perhaps the person who reads it next is someone who has been praying for a reason to believe that God has not given up on them.
And perhaps your simple act of sharing will be one small part of their journey toward the truth.
Now, return with me one final time to that troubled church in Corinth.
One man was living in scandal.
A congregation was refusing to grieve.
And an apostle, writing from a distance, insisted that the church could no longer confuse indifference with love.
But he did not end his argument by pointing to the greatness of the church.
He pointed to Christ our Passover.
The sacrificed Lamb.
The Savior of sinners.
The One whose blood makes forgiveness possible and whose resurrection announces that death and darkness do not have the final word.
That is why the church must never make peace with sin.
And that is why the church must never lose hope for sinners.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that our failures do not matter.
It is the announcement that our failures are so serious that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is so great that all who turn to Him in faith can be forgiven and made new.
So if you are the one who needs to repent, come to Jesus.
If you are the one who needs to confront someone, do it with truth, humility, and love.
If you are the one who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy, remember that the failures of Christ's followers do not change the righteousness of Christ Himself.
And if you are the one who has already repented but still cannot forgive yourself, remember that your hope rests not in the perfection of your past, but in the sufficiency of your Savior.
The man in Corinth was not beyond the reach of God's mercy.
Peter was not beyond it.
And no sinner who truly turns to Jesus needs to believe that their past is stronger than His saving grace.
The scandal may explain how you fell, but only Jesus Christ can give you the grace to rise—and the power to walk a different road.
